title: Authentication: Direct Query
subtitle: How a provider proves a caller ID is genuine by asking the caller’s own provider, in real time, during call setup.
endNote: Next, see the alternative: verifying calls with short-lived tokens.

segments.text: Today’s phone network has no reliable way to check who is really calling.
Caller ID can be spoofed in seconds. Anyone can claim to be anyone, even your bank.
The network passes the fake number straight through, and the customer sees it as genuine.
That single gap enables fraud on a massive scale.
PSTN2 closes that gap with a simple idea: ask.
Alpha Telecom receives a call. The caller ID is 0161 496 0123, a number held by Bravo Networks.
So Alpha asks Bravo directly: did you place this call?
Bravo gives a definitive, signed answer, typically within a hundred milliseconds.
Here is the flow in detail. First, Alpha finds the provider that holds the caller ID, using PSTN2 number discovery.
Then it sends Bravo a signed verification request, with the call details: the caller, the number called, and a call reference.
Bravo checks its own record of the calls it has just placed.
The call is there, so Bravo answers: verified. If it were not, Bravo would answer: not verified.
Either way, Alpha now knows for certain.

scenes.title: When the caller ID has been ported

segments.text: Numbers move between providers. So how does Alpha know which provider to ask?
This time the caller ID is 0113 496 0456. Ofcom’s numbering list names Charlie Comms as its Range Holder, so Alpha asks Charlie.
But the number has been ported to Bravo Networks. So Charlie answers with a redirect to Bravo.
Alpha sends its verification request to Bravo, the provider that holds the number today. Bravo confirms or denies the call.
If a cached answer is ever out of date, the provider replies: not held, invalidate your cache. Alpha rediscovers and retries, within five hops in total.
Verification happens in real time, typically in under a hundred milliseconds.
That fits comfortably inside normal call setup, so it is finished before the phone even rings.
The customer notices no delay. The experience is seamless.
Now watch a fraudster try. They spoof 0161 496 0123, Bravo’s number, and call an Alpha customer.
Alpha asks Bravo: did you place this call? Bravo has no record of it, so it answers: not verified.
Alpha can reject the call, or mark it as suspicious, before the customer’s phone even rings.
With direct query, spoofing a PSTN2 number simply stops working.

scenes.title: A definitive answer, not a confidence level

segments.text: STIR/SHAKEN, used in North America, takes a different approach.
It attaches an attestation level, A, B or C, which says how confident the originating carrier is.
PSTN2 gives a definitive answer: yes, we placed this call, or no, we did not.
STIR/SHAKEN also needs a certificate infrastructure, with authorities, certificates and governance to run.
PSTN2 uses direct, signed messages between providers. Each provider simply publishes its own keys.
Every verification query travels over an encrypted TLS 1.3 connection.
Every message is signed with Ed25519, so it cannot be forged or altered. A unique message ID and timestamp stop replays.
Rate limits protect each provider from floods of queries.
And every request is logged, so failed and suspicious checks leave an audit trail.
The system is designed to stay resilient under attack.
For a provider, implementation means one API endpoint.
When a request arrives, it checks the provider’s own record of recent calls, and returns a signed answer.
No central database is needed, and there is no certificate authority to run.
Just direct queries between providers, found through Ofcom’s numbering lists.
Deployed across the major providers, PSTN2 authentication could cut fraud rates by eighty percent or more.
Victims would be protected, and fraudsters stopped.
Trust in phone calls would be restored, using technology that is available today.
